children: Here's a number worth sitting with: Americans with the lowest levels of financial literacy spend about 13 hours a week thinking about and dealing with money problems, according to a study published by the TIAA Institute. Those who score highest on the same financial literacy test spend roughly four hours a week on the same thing. That's not a small gap. That's nearly an entire workday, every single week, that some people are losing to money stress that others simply aren't.
It's Not Really a Knowledge Problem

The instinct here is to assume the fix is obvious: learn more about money, and you'll spend less time stressing about it. But that's not quite right, and it's worth understanding why before you go sign up for another course. Christine Benz, director of personal finance and retirement planning at Morningstar, points to a more likely explanation: scarcity. People spending 13 hours a week on their finances aren't usually doing it because they lack information. They're doing it because they're actively juggling — moving money between accounts to cover a bill, negotiating with a creditor, figuring out which payment can wait another few days. Doug Boneparth, a certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, frames the underlying stress a little differently: it's not complexity that wears people down, it's open loops. Unresolved questions, tasks that haven't been automated, decisions that never got scheduled and just sit there generating a low-grade hum of anxiety in the background. The fix isn't knowing more — it's closing those loops so they stop needing your attention at all. Here's how to actually do that.
1. Build a Buffer Before Anything Else
If you're stuck in a cycle of constantly worrying about money,
make an emergency fund — even a small one — your No. 1 financial priority

, ahead of every other goal on your list. The standard target is three to six months of expenses, which can feel out of reach if you're already stretched thin. But even a partial cushion changes the math on stress. The logic is straightforward: once you have a buffer, a flat tire or a surprise copay stops being an emergency that eats into your week. It becomes a line item you already planned for.
2. Automate Everything You Possibly Can
If building a buffer is the foundation,
automation is the fastest way to shrink your weekly money-time after that

. It's the lowest-hanging fruit available: auto-pay your bills, your subscriptions, your debt payments. It's a one-time setup that then requires zero weekly maintenance. Once your cash cushion is solid, extend the same logic to your savings and investing — automatic transfers that move money toward your goals before you ever have the chance to decide whether to spend it instead. If you never see the money move, you never have to make a decision about it. It's already handled. It also helps to shrink the number of accounts you're juggling in the first place. Every extra account or credit card is one more thing to check, reconcile, and worry about. A single aggregator app that shows your full financial picture — spending, saving, investments, debt — in one view can take a genuine chunk of that mental overhead off your plate.
3. Get Targeted Help, Not Encyclopedic Knowledge

There's a limit to what automation and a cash buffer can solve on their own. Eventually you'll hit a financial situation — a job loss, an inheritance, a health scare — that no amount of automatic transfers fully prepares you for. When that happens, the smarter move isn't trying to become an expert in everything. Surya Kolluri of the TIAA Institute makes the case for targeted knowledge over comprehensive knowledge:
focus on what's actually relevant to your current life stage

. Younger workers get the most value from understanding saving habits and long-term investing. Older workers closer to retirement get more value studying the specifics of claiming Social Security. If you want outside help, check what your employer already offers — many companies provide financial wellness resources and retirement plan guidance that go unused simply because people don't think to look. Pro bono financial planning events in your community are another option, though it's worth staying alert to which advisors are there to genuinely help and which are using the event to find new clients.
The Goal Was Never to Become a Financial Expert

You don't need to master personal finance to stop losing hours to it every week. You need fewer open loops, a buffer that keeps small emergencies small, and just enough targeted knowledge for wherever you are in life right now. Do that, and the
13 hours starts looking a lot more like four
. That's a full workday back — every single week.
